newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian balance of payments deficit widens in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Russian balance of payments deficit widens in 1996.

text.p: Russia's overall balance of payments deficit, reflecting the net losses of its financial and trade transactions with the rest of the world, doubled to $22.6 billion in 1996, according to official figures.
The Central Bank, and the Russian European Centre for Economic Policy (RECEP), said the current account surplus, the balance of trade and services, narrowed to $9.3 billion from $9.5 billion in 1995.
The capital account deficit, net investment and debt outflows, doubled to $24.1 billion.

Russia had to spend $2.8 billion of currency reserves, borrow $3.8 billion from the International Monetary Fund and $4.7 billion from other international financial institutions and governments to finance the 1996 deficit, RECEP said.
Russia also rescheduled or deferred $11.1 billion of former borrowings, so debt service was $7.1 billion.

The Central Bank and RECEP, itself quoting central bank data, issued the following figures in billions of dollars, for transactions with all countries, including Baltic states and members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Use of IMF credits and loans 3.8 5.5
NOTES - *IFIs -- international financial institutions. Differences due to rounding. RECEP and investment bank Renaissance Capital provided the following notes.
Trade balance, foreign direct investment and portfolio investment into Russia improved strongly in the fourth quarter.
Non-factor services net -- includes net tourism figure of -$5.1 billion in 1996, comprising $5.5 billion tourism receipts and $10.1 billion spending by Russian tourists abroad.
Portfolio investment liabilities -- of the $7.5 billion invested in Russian securities in 1996, $5.2 billion came in the fourth quarter.
Hard currency cash -- purchases of dollars by Russian households who typically hold savings in cash at home. Figure -8.5 shows households bought $8.5 billion of cash dollars.
Bank accounts and deposits -- additional savings placed in foreign-currency accounts, mainly by households.
Trade credits -- credits mainly to countries still relying on cheap supplies of Russian natural resources.

Overdue payments -- shows payments not made on Russian exports and credits, including non-payment for Russian energy by former Soviet republics and other East European countries. The figure of -9.5 shows an accrual of assets in this way.
Non-repatriated export revenue -- the figure of 4.2 reflects profits of natural resource exporters legally removed from export receipts and kept in foreign currency.
Loans received -- figure of 6.4 shows loans received and unpaid debts falling due during the year.
Errors and omissions -- could reflect illegal capital flight.
